title: Predictive occupancy smoother + bounded preemption (PRD - draft)
content:
Problem statement:

Our Dedicated customers need predictable latency and capacity guarantees, but spikes in short-lived traffic and bursty patterns cause repeated soft-evictions and reactive preemptions that degrade UX and increase support load. Existing approaches (static headroom, burst credits, simple autoscalers) either over-provision (costly) or respond too late (bad UX). We need a mechanism that smooths short-term occupancy while limiting tenant-visible preemption to a bounded and transparent window.

Summary / proposal: Predictive Occupancy Smoother + Bounded Preemption

- Introduce a per-tenant short-horizon occupancy predictor (30s-15m window) that feeds an occupancy-smoothing controller which adjusts soft headroom and preemption thresholds proactively.
- Implement a bounded preemption policy: when capacity pressure requires preemption, the system applies degradations only within a configurable, documented time window (e.g., 60–300s), with explicit fallbacks and a maximum retry/backoff per tenant to avoid oscillation.
- Provide tenant-side degradation profiles (latency-first, quality-first, token-shed) that map to safe runtime behaviors (reduce batch sizes, lower concurrency, quantized variants, model fallbacks).
- Expose an admin UI and policy API for customers and Redwood operators to set smoothing aggressiveness, preemption windows, and allowed fallback families.

Why this is different: 
- Instead of purely reactive autoscaling or credit-based bursting, we predict short spikes and smooth the allocation curve, reducing the number and severity of preemptions.
- Bounded preemption ensures predictable, time-limited customer impact and simpler SLO reasoning for both product and SRE.

Goals (what success looks like):

1) Reduce customer-facing soft-evictions by 40% on bursty workloads (measured by traces with eviction events).
2) Reduce 95th-percentile request latency increase during load spikes by 20% compared to today.
3) Keep incremental cost delta for typical customers below 6% (via improved utilization rather than simply adding headroom).
4) Provide clear telemetry so customers can see when smoothing or bounded preemption acted on their traffic.

Non-goals:

- This is not a substitute for long-term capacity planning or reserved pool sizing.
- Not intended to replace Dedicated’s existing committed burst credit accounting; it complements it.

Target personas / user stories:

- Platform engineer (Customer): "I want my product to avoid sudden rate-limited errors during traffic spikes without buying extra committed capacity for the entire season."
- Infra SRE (Redwood): "I want predictable, observable preemption events that are bounded in time so we can document and mitigate their operational impact."
- Product manager (Redwood): "I want a measurable reduction in support tickets related to transient preemptions and clearer billing signals when smoothing increased cost usage."

High-level design:

1) Short-horizon predictor
   - Input signals: per-tenant request rate, sequence length distribution, recent queue/backlog, model family, region, historical diurnal patterns, and external signals (customer-configured seasonality windows).
   - Lightweight model: initially an exponential smoothing + AR(1) fallback with tunable half-life; iterate to probabilistic quantile forecaster (online quantile regression) if needed.
   - Output: predicted occupancy percentiles (P50/P90/P95) for 30s, 2m, 5m, 15m horizons.

2) Smoother controller
   - Policy converts forecasts into soft headroom adjustments and throttling levers: small proactive capacity reservations, temporary concurrency caps, or promotion of cached responses.
   - Aggressiveness knob per-tier: conservative (enterprise), default (self-serve), aggressive (experimental).

3) Bounded preemption policy
   - Preemption is only allowed when predicted occupancy exceeds physical capacity and smoothing cannot avoid it.
   - When preemption is triggered: apply degradation to a tenant for a bounded window (configurable default: 120s). Within that window, do not escalate (no full evictions). After window ends, the tenant is eligible for recovery with backoff.
   - Track per-tenant preemption budget (max windows per hour/day) to avoid starvation.

4) Degradation profiles (customer-selectable)
   - latency-first: reduce concurrency and prefer lower-latency model variants; may increase token-cost efficiency but lower quality.
   - quality-first: prefer model fallbacks that keep throughput with minimal quality loss; accept higher latency within SLOs.
   - token-shed: truncate long generations early and prioritize short requests (good for high-volume chatbots).

5) Interfaces and controls
   - Product Console: smoothing insights view, recent preemption windows, recommended aggressiveness.
   - API: PATCH /dedicated/{tenant}/smoothing { mode, aggressiveness, allowed_fallbacks, preempt_window_seconds }
   - Alerts: automatic email/console notices when a bounded preemption window is triggered for a customer, with root-cause hint (forecasted spike vs sudden unpredicted surge).

Operational details / telemetry:

- Signals to emit: predictor_confidence (Pxx), smoothing_actions (reserve_cpus_gpus, concurrency_cap), preemption_events (start_ts, end_ts, reason, profile), customer_impact_estimate (latency_delta, token_loss_estimate).
- Dashboards: per-region dedicated-capacity heatmap, preemption frequency chart, occupancy forecast overlay, tenant impact timeline.
- SLIs: preemption_rate_per_1000_requests, mean_preemption_window_length, %requests_served_during_preemption.

Algorithm notes and safety: 

- Start conservative: predictor calibrated to under-forecast rather than over-forecast to limit wasted headroom.
- Implement safety cutoff: when predictor confidence is low, fall back to current autoscaler behavior (no proactive reservations).
- Limit scope initially to a small subset of Dedicated pools (canary rollout) and only to tenants who opt-in or are in an experimental tier.

API & config surface (initial):

- tenant.smoothing.enabled: bool
- tenant.smoothing.mode: [off, conservative, default, aggressive]
- tenant.smoothing.preempt_window_sec: integer (60–900)
- tenant.smoothing.allowed_fallbacks: list of model_family ids
- tenant.smoothing.max_windows_per_hour: integer

Rollout plan:

1) Prototype (Q1 2026): internal-only in a single test pool; run predictor in passive mode (record-only) to tune parameters.
2) Canary (Q2 2026): enable smoothing in conservative mode for 5% of dedicated pools (ops-chosen) and surface console telemetry.
3) Opt-in beta (Q3 2026): allow selected customers to opt into smoothing; collect feedback and measure success metrics.
4) Gradual opt-out default (Q4 2026): make smoothing default for self-serve tenants in default mode if telemetry supports it; enterprise kept conservative by default.

Runbook (operator-facing):

- When a bounded preemption window is active: check predictor_confidence and smoothing_actions traces. If confidence is low and high customer impact observed, disable smoothing for that pool and open DED-incident.
- If preemption windows exceed configured budgets: escalate to capacity-ops and consider temporary pool expansion or targeted migrates.

Open questions / risks:

- Forecast error cost: how much headroom is acceptable? Initial configuration should favor utilization gains but we need a hard budget guard.
- Customer trust: customers may reject any system that proactively changes runtime behavior. We need clear transparency and easy opt-out controls.
- Complexity vs ops overhead: predictor + controller + UI increases product surface—need to confirm SRE staffing for new alerting.
- Interactions with burst credits and reserved capacity: ensure bounded preemption does not double-count or unfairly penalize tenants using burst credits.

Privacy / compliance notes:

- Predictor uses aggregated per-tenant telemetry only; no user PII. Customer-configured seasonality signals may not contain sensitive data; document allowed fields.

Next steps / action items (owners):

- Infra prototype: build passive predictor collector and smoothing controller (Diego) — DED-2387 (ETA: 2026-01-15).
- UX/Console: design smoothing insights page and alerts (Nora) — UX-1073 (ETA: 2026-02-10).
- API & Billing: define billing semantics for proactive reservations (Liam) — BILL-559 (ETA: 2026-02-28).
- Legal/Compliance: quick review on telemetry retention (Ayesha) — LEG-88 (ETA: 2026-01-30).

Notes / rough ideas to iterate on:

- Consider a hybrid credit model: smoothing uses ephemeral reservation credits funded by small per-minute microcharges to customers that opt-in, to align incentives.
- Explore integrating with Optimize recommendations: if smoothing consistently buys headroom for a tenant, propose a reserved capacity offer.

Appendix: quick experiment plan

- Passive collect (2 weeks): gather predictor signals across 10 pools; compute forecast accuracy and the false-positive headroom cost.
- Micro-canary (4 weeks): enable conservative smoothing for one pool; measure customer impact and preemption reduction.
